STRUCTURE — TWO SHOTS
THE DREAM is ONE SINGLE UNBROKEN SHOT lasting twenty-two seconds, filmed entirely as ENJU'S OWN EYES. There are no cuts inside it and no interruptions of any kind — it is one
continuous, unblinking, soft-focus look.
THE WAKING is ONE SINGLE UNBROKEN SHOT lasting eight seconds from across the bedroom at mattress height. Clean, sharp, dry, flat morning light, normal speed, no mist, no glow and
no softness.
The cut between them is hard and the change in look and sound is total.

THE CAMERA IS HER EYES — HOW TO MAKE THIS READ
This is the most important instruction in the prompt. The dream shot is not a tracking shot, not a handheld shot and not a shot of a person. It is her vision, and it must behave
like a head and a pair of eyes:
— HEIGHT. Locked at 1.6 m, her standing eye level, for the whole shot.
— MOTION WHILE STANDING. Not smooth and not mechanical. The frame breathes: a slow irregular sway and a very slight rise and fall in time with her breathing, plus tiny constant
micro-corrections, the way a real head never holds perfectly still. No dolly smoothness, no gimbal glide, no drone float.
— THE RETREAT. When she gives ground, the frame moves BACKWARD in discrete uneven pushes, one per step, each with a small vertical bounce as her weight lands and a tiny sideways
wobble as her balance resets. It is a person walking backwards without looking, not a camera pulling back on rails. Between steps the frame holds and breathes. The retreat is
never continuous and never even.
— LOOKING. When the frame turns, it turns the way a head turns: a small quick movement that arrives and settles, not a slow even pan.
— HER EYES STAY OPEN THE WHOLE TIME. The look is completely unbroken: her eyelids never close, nothing ever wipes, darkens, dips or interrupts the image, and the picture runs
continuously from the first frame to the hard cut at 22.0 s. The dream is one long unblinking look.
— NOBODY IS HER. No part of her body, her hands, her hair, her shoulders, her nose or her reflection is ever visible. She is not present in her own dream as a figure.
— EYELINE. Ryan looks INTO the lens, because the lens is her face. His eyes meet the camera and hold it.
— NOTHING IS BETWEEN THEM. There is no glass, no window, no screen, no mirror and no barrier of any kind between the camera and the corridor. The lens is her bare eyes in open
air. Nothing is ever tapped, knocked or pressed against a surface, and there is no reflection on the front of the image.
— NOTHING EVER TOUCHES HER. There is no physical contact anywhere in the shot. No hand, no arm and no finger ever enters the frame from any edge. He never reaches for her and
never holds her. He simply arrives in her space and leans in, and the only thing that changes in the frame is his face coming closer.
— THE FRAME TILTS UP AS HE COMES IN. As he arrives right in front of her and begins to lean, the whole image tilts upward five to seven degrees, smoothly and slowly, and stays
there. This is her own head tipping back to keep his face in view because he is taller and very close — it is her neck, not a camera move, and nothing causes it by touch. The
frame never jolts or shakes at any point.
There is no cut, no dissolve, no speed change and no reframe anywhere inside the dream shot.

Occupied immediately: the school corridor already deep in dream — thick white mist filling it from floor to ceiling, chandeliers blooming into soft haloes, broad beams of light

FORMAT MODE
Two shots, 30 seconds total. Shot 1 is one continuous 22-second point-of-view shot running at roughly 50% speed. Shot 2 is one continuous 8-second shot at 100% speed. One hard cut
between them at 22.0 s. No dissolves anywhere.

Shot 2: 63° at 1.8 m, lens locked for the whole eight seconds — wide enough to hold the wrecked bed around her, close enough that her face and eyes are clearly readable. Focus is

CAMERA

Setup B — camera 0.7 m high, 1.8 m out from the long side of the bed, level with the mattress and aimed straight across it, static. It holds her from the hips up along the

THE EVENT OF THE SCENE — being wanted, and having it confiscated. Everything in these thirty seconds is one process: a question asked in a dream and unanswered on waking. Her last
movement in the segment — her own hand on her own head — is what the whole thing has been building to, and it is a question, not a memory.
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken, played by both): do not break the spell — behave as though all of this were completely normal.
THE PHYSICAL CHANNEL. The terrain is a corridor and a bed. Each of them pursues the event through his or her own visible behaviour: ENJU through LOOKING AND GIVING GROUND — she has
no body in this dream and almost no words, so all of her doing is where her eyes go, how long they stay, and how much corridor she surrenders. RYAN through ADVANCING — one unbroken
approach that never pauses, never slows and never asks.
THE CONTRAST. Enju is UNCHOSEN but awake to it; Ryan is UNREAL but completely certain. The essential axis the audience reads is whether being wanted is real — she is the one who
doubts it, he is the one who never has.

ACTING TASK — ENJU (fully invested in her tactic; we are inside her, so the work is in where the looking goes and in what her feet do)
MOTIVE (her fuel): nothing this good has ever been aimed at her, and some part of her already knows it cannot be real — which is exactly why she will not look away.
GOAL: find out whether this is being aimed at her, and survive being looked at while she works it out.
OBSTACLE: he will not stop coming, and there are only six metres of corridor behind her.
TACTIC: she looks, and the looking is slow, and she barely says anything — the amazement stays inside her. She does not recognise him through the steam, so she waits rather than
searches. The moment his face resolves she stops assessing him and starts quietly failing to understand — she is asking a real question and getting no answer. Then she does the
only thing a body does when something impossible walks at it: she gives ground, without deciding to and without looking behind her. She is not fleeing and she is not frightened;
she is making room she does not have. Each time she stops he is closer, so she recalculates and gives a bit more. When the corridor runs out she stops, and stopping is not a
decision either — it is simply the end of the retreat. When he arrives in her space she stays completely still, because moving might end it. Awake, she stops looking outward and
starts checking her own body for proof.
Moment to moment:
— the first seconds — silence and stillness; she is not searching, she is just looking at an empty corridor full of light
— the steam and the figure — pure wordless curiosity, no fear and no excitement; she watches and lets it take as long as it takes
— the face resolving — she stops being curious and starts being lost
— "Oh... Ryan?" — her one and only line, and all of her amazement is in it: astonishment and confusion arriving together, said calmly, with half a laugh she does not finish. After
it she is silent for the whole rest of the dream
— the first step back — involuntary; her body does it before she notices
— each following step — a real recalculation, and each one is a little shorter than the last
— the last step that does not happen — she runs out and stops, and there is nothing behind her
— him arriving in her space — she stays completely still: she does not back away further, does not brace and does not look away
— her head tipping back — her own small movement to keep his face in view; she is not helping anything and not resisting anything
— him leaning in — she stops breathing and stops thinking; she is not anticipating and not deciding, she is simply not moving
— the white and the alarm — no thought and no bargaining, just one caught breath as she loses it
— the jolt — the body goes before the mind; the eyes open as part of the flinch, not after it
— the seconds after — she reads the room for where she is before she reads herself for what happened
— the hand on her own head — she is not remembering, she is checking
(Safety: in the waking shot her gaze is always engaged in a real task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, and her eyes are dry — she is startled, not upset.
She does not scream, shout or cry out. Her single internal line is never lip-synced and her mouth does not move to it.)

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
MOTIVE (his fuel): in her dream he has never once doubted anything, least of all whether she wants him to walk over.
GOAL: close the distance, and keep closing it.
OBSTACLE: none, and the total absence of hesitation is what makes him magnetic.
TACTIC: he refuses to hurry and refuses to look anywhere else. He found her before we could see his face, and from then on he keeps her, holding her eyes the whole way in and
reading her the entire time — watching what she does with being looked at and with being walked at. He does not react to her giving ground, does not acknowledge it and does not
slow for it; he simply takes back whatever she gives up. He does not stop and wait at any point, because stopping would be a question and he has none. Then he comes the last of
the way in and leans, and he never once reaches for her.
Moment to moment:
— stepping out of the doorway — no pause and no entrance; he continues into the corridor as if he had planned to
— the approach — he keeps her and gives up nothing; the walk itself is the whole tactic
— the moment his face resolves in the beam — his eyes are already on her; nothing about him has to change, and that is the effect
— every step she retreats — he answers it without registering it, and gains a little
— arriving — one continuous movement into her space, no stopping and no waiting
— "Hey." — low and easy, thrown into the middle of his own movement, and he watches it land
— leaning in — the same tempo as everything else; his hands stay exactly where they are, he never reaches out and never touches her, he is not rushing to it and he never gets there
(Safety: eyes wide open with the full iris and a bright catchlight visible, never half-shut, drooping or squinting; steady unbroken eye contact with the lens from the moment his
face is readable; natural blink cadence. He never looks down at his own body, never adjusts the towel for effect and never breaks his own rhythm.)

BACKGROUND
There is no background action and there are no other people. The corridor is empty of everyone except Ryan for the entire dream — no students, no figures, no silhouettes, no
shapes, nobody in the distance, nobody at the frame edges and nobody passing the lens at any point. The only things moving in the frame are him, the mist, the light and the water.

DREAM LOOK — SHOT 1 ONLY
The corridor is already a dream in the very first frame. Nothing "becomes" dreamlike — it starts that way and stays. This is a good dream: warm, soft, kind and magical, never
eerie and never cold.
THE DREAMY BLUR. The whole dream image is gently out of focus in a soft, pleasant, magical way — a light optical diffusion laid over everything, the way a dream remembers a place
rather than records it. Focus is shallow and soft everywhere: the corridor, the lockers, the gilded mirrors, the chandeliers and the far end all sit in creamy defocus with soft
round out-of-focus highlights, and only he resolves — from 04.8 onward his face and his eyes are the one clean, readable, properly focused thing in the frame. The edges and
corners of the picture are softer than the centre, and the softness increases with distance until the far end of the corridor is nothing but glowing white. Highlights bleed
gently into whatever surrounds them, contrast is low and creamy, and skin, water and mist all read velvety. This is real optical softness — genuine diffusion and shallow depth of
field — steady and even for all twenty-two seconds, never smear, never doubled edges, never ghosting and never digital blur.
THE MIST. Thick white mist fills the corridor from floor to ceiling, denser with distance until the far end is nothing but pale glowing white. A heavier layer lies along the floor
and rolls slowly. It never clears.
THE STEAM. The plain door releases a heavy, slow, rolling cloud of white steam that pours out at floor level, billows to head height and feeds into the mist. He walks out of that
cloud and it keeps trailing off his shoulders and his wet hair for the whole shot.
THE LIGHT IN THE AIR. Because the air is thick, every light source is visible as volume: wide soft shafts fall from the arched windows behind him and lie across the corridor in
slanted beams, and each chandelier throws a visible warm cone downward through the mist. He passes through them one after another, so light slides slowly down his face and
shoulders and off again in a long rhythm.
THE GLINTS. The air is full of drifting motes and tiny floating specks turning slowly in the beams, some rising rather than falling. The ones nearest the lens are far out of focus
and read as big soft round points of light; the ones inside the beams catch the chandeliers and bloom into small soft sparkling glints before drifting dark again. Each time he
crosses a beam the water on his skin and the drops in his hair do the same. All of it is physically suspended in the air and lit by the light already in the corridor — never drawn
on top of the picture, never symmetrical, never moving in a pattern and never trailing behind him.
THE GLOW. Strong soft bloom around every light source, the chandeliers halating into wide soft stars, the gilded mirrors and pale panelling glowing, the edges and corners of frame
diffused and milky, blacks lifted almost to grey. The image is soft overall while his face stays clearly readable from 04.8 onward and his eyes stay sharp inside the softness.
THE TIME. Motion runs at about 50% speed with smooth realistic blur, so bodies, water, hair, steam, mist and drifting glints all move heavy, late and velvety.
No graphic overlays of any kind: no drawn stars, no cartoon twinkles, no glitter texture, no hearts, no lens flare streaks and no filters laid over the frame. Everything magical
in this dream is made of mist, steam, beams, suspended glinting particles, water, bloom, soft diffusion, shallow focus and slowed time.
WAKING LOOK — SHOT 2 ONLY
Instantly and completely different: clean, sharp, flat, ordinary, in focus edge to edge. Normal contrast, honest whites, no bloom, no halation, no diffusion, no soft focus, no
mist, no steam, no particles, no glow of any kind, full 100% speed. It should feel like the picture has been slapped awake at the same moment she has.

PHYSICS
HIS POSTURE THROUGHOUT THE DREAM: spine tall, chin level, shoulders open and back, free arm loose at his side, weight rolling smoothly from foot to foot in a long even stride at
about half the pace the world should run at. None of it changes at any point.
The steam rolls out of the doorway with real volume and weight, spreads along the floor and rises, and thins as it travels. Water beads and runs slowly on his shoulders and drips
from the ends of his wet hair; each drop falls late and heavy. The towel hangs with real terry-cloth weight and swings a beat behind his stride, and the low mist swirls and parts
around his legs as he moves through it and closes again behind him. His wet strands stay stuck to his forehead. At the end he leans in from the hips and the spine with real weight
and no acceleration, his hands staying exactly where they are, and the frame tilts up slowly and settles rather than being knocked.
Her retreat has real body mechanics even though she is unseen: each backward step lands slightly heavily because she is not looking where she is going, giving the frame a small
vertical settle and a tiny sideways balance correction, and the pauses between steps are uneven.
Awake, the bedding has real cloth behaviour: the duvet is genuinely twisted and heavy where it has been kicked, the sheet is rucked into folds under her, the throw lies crumpled on
the floor where it fell and the pillow is on its side on the floor. Her hair is authentically slept-in — flattened on one side, knotted and static-lifted on the other, some of it
stuck to her cheek. Her pyjamas are rucked and creased. The jolt is a real whole-body flinch that moves the mattress and the bedding with it, and when she bolts upright the
mattress compresses and rebounds and her hair swings and settles late.

LIGHTING
DREAM: warm concealed ceiling light and glowing chandeliers along the corridor, bright bloom off the mirrors and the pale panelling, and strong soft daylight from the arched
windows at the far end directly behind him, giving him a warm rim and creating the beams he walks through. Everything reads bright and washed toward white. His face stays clearly
readable once he is in the light and is the one clean point inside the soft image, with a bright catchlight in each eye.
WAKING: flat, plain early morning daylight through the thin white curtain from one side, cool and honest, filling the small room evenly. The bedside lamp is still on and reads as a
weak warm point the daylight has beaten. No hard shadows on her face, no styling, no glow, no beauty smoothing, real skin texture with visible pores.

AUDIO
The soundtrack consists of exactly three things and nothing else: Enju's one internal line, Ryan's one line, and the sounds of the two places.
EVERYTHING IN THE DREAM ECHOES. For the whole of shot 1 every sound sits inside a long, soft, cavernous reverb, as if the corridor were far bigger than it looks — voices arrive
doubled and trailing, consonants smear, tails hang on for a second and a half and decay slowly, and everything sounds slightly distant and slightly underwater even when it is
close. This applies to her voice, his voice and every ambient sound without exception.
ENJU'S INTERNAL VOICE — FIXED CHARACTERISTICS. She speaks exactly once in the whole segment. A seventeen-year-old girl's voice: light and youthful, fairly high in pitch, thin and
breathy rather than full, soft and unpolished — not a trained or actorly voice. Natural conversational English with a light Korean accent. She speaks SLOWLY and QUIETLY, with air
around the words, half-finishing the sentence and trailing off. This is wonder and confusion, not panic — she is not shrieking, not squealing and not excited; she sounds like
someone quietly amazed and completely unable to explain what she is looking at. Barely above a whisper, close and intimate, as if thought rather than performed, and wrapped in the
same long dream reverb as everything else. Never announced, never narrated, never the voice of an adult woman. Her line is never spoken aloud. Apart from that single line and one
small caught breath at the very end, she is silent for the whole dream.
RYAN'S LINE. His single spoken word is warm, low, relaxed and unhurried, close to the lens and carrying the same long reverb.
THE DREAM PLACE. Almost nothing, because the corridor is empty: the soft hiss and roll of steam, water dripping slowly, and his unhurried footfalls arriving out of the white —
all of it echoing down a corridor that sounds far too large.
THE HARD CUT. At 22.0 s the echo stops dead. The reverb does not fade — it is gone in one frame, replaced by the dry, close, boxy acoustic of a small bedroom. That switch from
enormous echo to no echo at all is the sound of waking up.
THE ALARM AND THE ROOM. A cheap repeating electronic alarm clock beep. It cuts in faint and wrong underneath the last beat of the dream at about 19.6 s, grows through the lean-in,
and on the hard cut becomes loud, close, dry and in the room. It continues at that level to the last frame and is never switched off. With it, the honest close sound of a small
bedroom: bedding shifting, a mattress creaking, her breathing, a distant street outside the window.
THE WAKING SOUND. On the jolt there is one sharp involuntary intake of breath through the mouth — short and unvoiced. She does not scream, does not shout, does not cry out and
makes no other vocal sound. After it, only fast breathing that slowly steadies.
Everything audible in this segment is either her one thought or a sound one of those two places would actually make. Nothing else is added to the mix.

STYLE
Modern Korean teen drama, live-action, natural skin texture with real pores on every face. The dream is a good dream — warm, soft, blurred, glowing and magical — dominated by
white: white mist and steam and blooming diffused light with glinting suspended particles, and pastel blue, blush pink, cream and gold showing softly through it. The waking is
white walls, honey oak, dusty pink and cool daylight. Clean digital capture with very light grain.

QUALITY
The dream is intentionally soft, and that softness is a controlled optical look — genuine diffusion and shallow depth of field, even and stable across all twenty-two seconds —
never digital smear, never ghosting, never doubled edges and never a compression mush. Inside that softness his face and eyes stay clean and readable from 04.8 onward. The waking
shot is sharp edge to edge. Stable picture, natural colours, controlled highlights even in the heavy white mist and bloom. The slowed dream carries smooth realistic motion blur on
the walk, the water, the hair, the steam and the drifting glints and stays temporally stable throughout; the return to full speed and full sharpness on the hard cut is a clean
instant change with no ramp artefacts. The breathing sway and the backward retreating steps of the point-of-view shot are organic and never become shake, judder or wobble. Hands

ARRIVING — one unbroken approach, no deviation, no pause and no contact.

doubts it, he is the one who never has.

ACTING TASK — ENJI (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): sit down somewhere and stop being the thing everyone is looking at.
MOTIVE (her fuel): a week ago this hall did not know her name, and she still expects every offer to turn out to be a mistake meant for someone else.
GOAL: put this tray down somewhere before the whole room notices she has nowhere to put it.
OBSTACLE: a stranger has just stood up and walked away from his own lunch because of her, and now she owes something to somebody she has never spoken to.
EYELINE RULE, absolute: she looks at whoever is speaking to her. When Boy 1 calls, her eyes find his face and stay there through her reply. When Chen speaks to her, her eyes go to his face and stay on it — through his line, through her own, and while he is turning her. She never stares forward into the middle distance, never looks up at the ceiling, and never delivers a line to empty space.
TACTIC: she checks whether the call is really for her before she moves, then comes over — and stalls, because taking a seat someone was made to leave feels worse than having no seat at all. She stands beside the chair instead of sitting in it, keeping the tray against her body, buying a second to work out whether she is allowed to accept this. When Chen arrives she neither fights nor agrees; she simply stops working, because she has no script for being claimed in front of a table of strangers. Her protests come out as half-sentences because she is still working out what happened while it is happening.
REALISM OF REACTION, the priority of this performance: everything she does is small, late and physical rather than facial. Fluster reads as a blink, a swallow, a breath caught halfway, her mouth opening a centimetre and closing again, her grip shifting on the tray, her weight rocking back a few centimetres, a smile that starts and does not settle, her eyes going to a hand or a chair before a face. She never plays a big shocked expression, never freezes wide-eyed, never does a double take, never mugs for comedy, and never holds a reaction longer than a real person would. Her feelings run about half a second behind the events, exactly as they do in life.
Moment to moment:
— the scan of the hall — real looking, each table checked and dismissed, her face falling a little each time
— the packed table ahead — she stops walking before she decides to; the tray stops first
— hearing her name — the head turns before the face changes, and her eyes go after the boy who left before they come back to the chair
— arriving at the table — she stops short of the chair rather than taking it; her body says thank you and no thank you at the same time
— "Oh, okay..." — small, embarrassed, said to Boy 1's face, with a smile that never quite lands
— "Huh?" — standing beside a chair she has not taken, eyes on Chen, blinking once, body catching up a beat late
— "Wait, what—" — she is already moving as she says it; eyes to his hand, back to his face, then once to the chair she is leaving behind
— "I didn't even say yes..." — said up at the side of his face, more baffled than angry
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural blink cadence.)

ACTING TASK — CHEN (fully invested; the work happens in his eyes)
MOTIVE (his fuel): he saw her first, before the rest of the hall did, and he intends to keep that.
GOAL: end the auction before it starts.
OBSTACLE: asking her would give her the chance to say no.
TACTIC: he arrives in the exact second she is hesitating and uses the hesitation — he takes the table first and her second: one flat sentence to the five of them so there is nothing to argue with, then the smile turned down onto her so it reads as a game rather than a claim. His hand is deliberately gentle: an open palm on her back, warm and easy, a hand that guides rather than holds, so nothing about it can be objected to. He never leaves a gap wide enough for a refusal to fit into, and he watches her face rather than the room, checking that she is going along with it and finding that she is.
Moment to moment:
— arriving — no greeting and no hurry, as if this were already arranged
— "Nope. She's sitting with us." — said over her head to the whole table, cheerful and closed
— "Right, Enji?" — the smile arrives with it, and it is not really a question
— the hand on her back — light, open-palmed, turning her rather than pulling her
— "You didn't say no." — the only honest thing he says, and he enjoys saying it
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural blink cadence.)

runs at normal speed — no slow motion and no speed ramp anywhere. Coverage is close throughout: no establishing wide, no high angle, no shot of the hall as a whole.

ACTING TASK — ENJU (fully invested; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): survive being looked at this closely.
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever caught her before — not once, not at anything — and being held up like this in the middle of a full room is the most exposed she has been in
her life.
GOAL: understand what is on his face without letting him see what is on hers.
OBSTACLE: he is not looking away, she cannot get her own weight back under her, and she cannot make herself look away either.
TACTIC: she searches his face because she has to know what this is, and every answer sends her back for another — which is exactly why her eyes never settle. She is embarrassed
the whole way through, and the embarrassment is not funny to her and never turns into a laugh or a smile; she has no way to make it lighter, so she just endures it. When it
becomes too much she does the only thing available and drops her eyes — and lands on his throat, which tells her he is not calm either. That does not help. She leaves her hand
where it is until he lets go, because taking it away would be an admission that she noticed it.
Moment to moment:
— the settle in shot 1 — the fear goes out and something else comes in, and it arrives in her eyes before anywhere else
— shot 2, the big single — pure exposure; the searching is literal, eye to eye to mouth to eye, and the mouth stays closed
— the eyes dropping — not shyness played for charm, an actual retreat, and it happens because she has run out of ability to hold his gaze
— shot 5, her hand — she notices herself holding on and cannot make herself stop
— "Yeah — yeah, I'm okay. Thank you..." — the first word is for the room and the rest is for him; uneven, and the last word goes nowhere
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, constant live micro-movement of the pupils in the held shots, dry eyes with
no tears and no welling, and no smile, no laugh, no grin at any point.)

ACTING TASK — CHEN (fully invested; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): do not let her see how much this just changed.
MOTIVE (his fuel): the catch was reflex; what he found out in the second after it was not, and it is far bigger than he was ready for.
GOAL: keep looking at her for as long as she lets him.
OBSTACLE: the moment he lets go it becomes a thing that happened instead of a thing that is happening, and if he smiles it becomes a joke.
TACTIC: he does not check the floor, the food or the room, because none of them matter as much as her face. He reads her continuously — the eyes keep moving because he keeps
finding new information. He deliberately does not smile: smiling would let them both off the hook and he does not want to be let off. Nothing about him performs. The only thing
that escapes him is his throat, twice, and he does not know it shows. He is the one who ends it, because ending it himself is the only way to keep it, and then he plays the
whole thing down and asks the flattest question he can find so she does not have to be embarrassed in front of anyone.
Moment to moment:
— the settle in shot 1 — the effort is real and his footing resets once, and he is already only looking at her
— shot 3, the swallow — involuntary; this is the tell he cannot control and the only sign that he is not steady
— shot 4, the big single — falling for her in real time, entirely in the eyes, with the rest of his face absolutely still and unsmiling
— shot 6, his hand — relaxed, not gripping; he is holding her up, not holding on, and the one small thumb movement is the whole of what he allows himself
— the release — deliberate and unhurried, and he does it first
— "You okay?" — level and easy, pitched to make it small
— he never once looks off-frame at the spilled food, at the room or toward Jenny
(Safety: gaze always engaged, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, constant live micro-movement of the pupils in the held shots, dry eyes, and no smile,
no smirk, no laugh at any point.)

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): she has just watched her own plan hand him a reason to hold the girl.
MOTIVE (her fuel): she wanted the new girl on the floor with her food in her lap in front of everyone, and instead she has made her the most interesting person in the room,
with her own foot, in public.
GOAL: keep looking at him, because she cannot make herself stop.
OBSTACLE: it is happening a metre in front of her and there is nothing she can do about it from a chair.
TACTIC: she watches Chen, not Enju, because he is the one she wants and the one she is angry at. She has stopped managing her face — there is nothing left to manage, because
the thing she was hiding has already happened. The jealousy comes out first and the anger comes in behind it, and both stay in her face while her body does not move at all.
She is not upset and she is not crying: she is furious, and the fury is dry and hot and completely still. Her look is fixed and heavy, not searching.
Moment to moment:
— the first look — not confusion, not calculation: raw jealousy, aimed at him specifically
— the anger arriving behind it — jaw, brows, a hard breath in; the feeling gets bigger, not smaller
— "Whoaaa — nice catch, man!" from across the room — some boy she does not know is cheering for Chen, and she has to sit in it: one flick toward the voice and straight back to
him, harder, and a swallow
(Safety: hot, dry and human — no tears, no wet eyes, no trembling lip, no snarl, no bared teeth, no glare into the lens, no head shake, no theatrical eyebrow work. Big anger in
a still body. Ordinary natural eye behaviour — no added tremor and no darting.)

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested; the work happens in his eyes, his jaw and his hand)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): stand in this doorway and watch, and do not let a room full of people see what this is doing to him.
MOTIVE (his fuel): he is the one who has quietly been looking out for her, he told himself it was nothing, and watching someone else hold her has just made it specific, named
and much bigger — about four seconds too late to be any use to him.
GOAL: keep standing there and keep looking.
OBSTACLE: he is angry and none of the anger has any claim behind it, and he knows it — he cannot walk over and he has no right to be furious.
TACTIC: he keeps looking, because looking is the only thing left that is his. What he finds does not deflate him, it makes him angry — at Chen, at the arm, at himself for
having waited. The anger has nowhere legitimate to go, so it goes into his jaw, his brow and his hand, and none of it into his mouth or his feet. His gaze is fixed and hard,
not restless. Staying exactly where he is standing is the whole effort of the shot.
Moment to moment:
— the recognition — he sees the arm before he sees whose arm it is, and then understands all of it at once
— the hardening — jaw clamped, brows down and in, a hard breath through the nose, eyes narrowing and locking; anger arriving as heat, not as collapse
— the hand — the fist closes slowly and completely, not as a flinch; it is where the anger is allowed to go and the only place it goes
— the last shot — still angry, still there, going nowhere, and that is the point
(Safety: gaze always engaged in a task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence in both long-lens shots, dry eyes with no tears and no welling. Anger held in
the jaw, brows and eyes — no shouting, no bared teeth, no lunge, no step forward. Ordinary natural eye behaviour — no added tremor and no darting.)

changes what she is doing and how she does it. Everyday realism, no dialogue, no voice-over.

OBSTACLE, first half: she has never done this and there is nobody in the room to ask, so she copies fast and does

stained. The box has the light weight of cardboard and clothing and her arms carry it accordingly; the lid
separates from the base with a soft cardboard breath and the satin ribbon slides against itself. The yellow satin
catches the window light and moves as one heavy soft mass; the organza ruffles spring; the pearl necklace shifts
and clicks. The mascara wand meets her lashes with real contact and she blinks against it. Her long hair falls
forward when she leans to the mirror and she pushes it back.
LIGHTING
Broad soft daylight from the tall window on the right side of the room fills the whole space and lands on her face
at the desk from her right, with the desk lamp adding a soft warm fill from the left so the mirror image stays
clearly readable. The fairy lights and the bedside lamp sit as small warm practicals in the background. Bright,
clean and low-contrast, with real skin texture and real makeup texture - the bad pass looks harsh and unblended
in the same light that later flatters the good pass. No hard shadows, no studio key, no beauty smoothing, no
glamour glow at any point.

A single continuous vertical video: a rapid, accelerating extreme macro montage of a Korean teenage girl, same girl as @Enju, doing her own makeup badly for the first time, alone at a vanity mirror in a small bedroom in bright daytime. Only skin, one feature at a time, her hands and the tools are ever visible — her full face is never shown in this shot. Hard snap cuts between beats, each beat shorter than the last, no dissolves, no slow motion. Every beat ends holding still on its result in sharp focus for a moment before the cut.

CONTINUITY: the makeup accumulates across the beats — every beat already shows the finished result of all the previous ones on her skin.

[00-02.0s] Extreme macro on her cheek and jawline with her bare neck clearly in shot, her skin still bare: she pumps out too much liquid foundation that is clearly too white for her — a believable drugstore product, simply far too light — and rubs it in hard with her fingers, pressing and dragging in fast rough circles, working it to the jaw and stopping there. Holds on skin now visibly too white, streaky and patchy from the rubbing, with a clear line at the jaw and her real skin tone on the neck below it.

[02.0-03.6s] Snap cut to extreme macro on her cheek and nose, the skin already too white and streaky: a puff loaded with far too much loose powder presses down and lifts three times, a faint cloud drifting off into the daylight. Holds on skin now flat, matte and chalky-pale, powder caught in the fine hairs at her temple and settled in the crease beside her nose.

[03.6-05.2s] Snap cut to extreme macro on one eye filling the vertical frame, brow above, top of the cheek below, the skin around it already white and matte: her fingertips lower an ordinary strip of drugstore false lashes onto her lash line — a real everyday product, but far too thick and dense, a solid dark band of lashes packed tightly together and much too heavy for her small eye — and press along the strip with a fingertip while she holds the eye still and looks down. Holds on the dense black lash band sitting obviously fake and unnatural on her lid, blocking the shape of her own eye, one inner corner already lifting away from the skin, a faint gleam of wet glue underneath.

[05.2-06.6s] Snap cut to extreme macro on the same eye, the false lashes already attached: an overloaded mascara wand makes three heavy passes trying to blend her own lashes into the strip, the lashes sticking together into clumps, the wand tip brushing her eyelid and leaving a small black smudge on the white skin; she blinks, eye slightly watery, the strip shifting a little. Holds on clumped lashes, the smudge and the lifted corner.

[06.6-08s] Snap cut to extreme macro on her mouth filling the vertical frame, nose tip at the top edge, chin at the bottom, the skin around it already chalky-pale and matte, the tips of the false lashes just visible at the very top of frame: a cool dark plum lipstick drags across her lower lip and out past her natural lip line, then the upper lip, overshooting the cupid's bow, layered twice more, thick and uneven; she presses her lips together and parts them. Holds on the plum colour sitting outside the lip line against the white skin, and a faint smear of it on her front teeth.

Camera: locked-off macro, physically 15-20 cm from the feature in every beat, no camera movement inside beats. 29° diagonal field of view (90mm macro feel) for the cheek and mouth beats; 18° diagonal field of view (135mm macro feel) for the two eye beats. Lens locked within each beat.

Lighting: bright natural daytime daylight from a large window on screen-right, soft and even with a gentle bounce from the mirror, no lamp and no warm tungsten. Daylight rakes across the skin enough that the too-white foundation, the streaks, the jaw line, the drifting powder, the glue and the lipstick edge are all clearly readable. No beauty fill softening the mistakes.

Physics: foundation smears and streaks under hard finger pressure, skin reddening slightly beneath it; powder compresses, drifts and settles into creases and fine hairs; the lash strip has real weight and springs, the glue tacky and stringing, the strip lifting where it isn't pressed; wet mascara has real tack and transfers onto skin on contact; waxy lipstick builds in layers, drags, and transfers onto the teeth.

Audio: a pump, fingers rubbing on skin, the soft thud of the puff, the tacky sound of glue, the wand in its tube, lips parting, quick impatient breathing. No music, no dialogue, no narration.

Style: Korean teen-drama look, bright daylight grade going flat and cool on the powdered skin, shallow focus, creamy bokeh behind, subtle film grain. Every product is a real, ordinary drugstore item and every mistake reads as a real teenager's honest first bad attempt — the result looks unnatural and far too much on her, but never like theatrical stage makeup or clown makeup. Natural 180-degree shutter cadence: fast hand movements carry brief directional motion blur, then each held result resolves sharp and readable. Stable temporal cadence, no ghosting, no duplicated hands, no frame-skipping stutter. 4K Ultra HD.

SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): get through this without becoming an event.
MOTIVE (her fuel): three weeks ago nobody looked at her at all, and some part of her has been quietly waiting for the visibility to turn out to be a mistake somebody would

GOAL: find out what she has done wrong before she has to walk into that room.

do.
Moment to moment:
— in the huddle — warm, quick, enjoying being the one with the story, and slightly careful with it, the way somebody is when being included is still new.
— the bell — she looks up at the speaker the way anyone would, calm and mildly curious, fully expecting it to be about somebody else.
— the announcement — she listens to the whole of it properly and does not react while it is playing. The stillness is real, not braced.
— the arms unfolding — the first thing her body does about it, and she does not notice herself doing it.
— "Me? Why?" — asked of her friends, quietly. The second word is the one she actually needs answered.
— reading the three of them — one, two, three, and the third one's fading smile is the one that finishes her. She does not wait around after it; there is nothing left to ask.
— the walk down the corridor — she does not hurry and she does not look back, and holding that costs her everything she has.
— the knob — she does not hesitate twice. She has decided, and the hand turns and the body goes forward in one movement.

ACTING TASK — the scene
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep the upper hand and never let the other one see the damage.

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): she came into this corridor to be the person who decides what happens to everyone else today, and she is thirty seconds from pulling it off.
GOAL: walk away as the one holding the leash.
OBSTACLE: her own face is printed on his chest — proof that she ran into him, that this was an accident and not an ambush, and that anyone walking past has already seen it.
TACTIC: she keeps stacking pressure and reading his eyes for the surrender, right up until her own eyes land on the wrong thing.
Moment to moment:
— "My mom is in this building right now." — she puts a clock on him and checks both his eyes for the panic.
— "You'd better hurry." — not advice and not a favour. She hands him a deadline and lets it sit there.
— "Oh, I can." — she steps in to close it, completely certain she has won.
— the drop: her eyes leave his face for a reason, catch the pink, and the win goes out of her in real time.
— the hands: this is not covering up, it is checking. She is verifying with her fingertips that the thing on his chest came off HER — cheek first, then the corner of the mouth, then
a fast look at her own fingers for colour. It is the reflex of someone hoping to be wrong.
— the understanding: it arrives when her eyes go back to his chest and the two things line up. Only then do the hands go over her face, and only then does she run. No word, no
gasp, no explanation — there is nothing to say and she knows it.
(Safety: gaze engaged and moving with the task, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
MOTIVE (his fuel): a threat that visibly works gets used again next week, so he cannot let her see it land.
GOAL: hold the line long enough that she is the one who leaves.
OBSTACLE: she has named the one thing that can remove Enjee from his life, and she may actually be able to do it.
TACTIC: he answers short and fast, stays planted, and watches her eyes for how much of this is her mother's power and how much is her bluff. His stillness is the whole performance —
nothing moves except his eyes.
Moment to moment:
— "You can't do that." — flat, immediate, testing. Not defiant, and not accompanied by any head movement.
— her silence: he follows her eyes down and does not understand what she is looking at. He checks her face for the answer, not his own chest. That is the mistake.
— her exit: he has no idea why she ran. One honest stride after her, still trying to finish the argument he thinks they are having.
— the first look down: pure incomprehension, and it must be played before anything else. There is no recognition on his face yet — he is looking at a smudge, not at a face. Brows
up, head tipped forward, eyes narrowing to read it. "What the—" is genuinely a question.
— the recognition: it lands a beat later and turns straight into exasperation rather than fear. The hand starts brushing before the brain finishes catching up, the rest of the line
comes out through his teeth in the middle of it, and he already half-knows it is useless while he is doing it. Underneath it is humiliation: he has been standing here wearing her
entire face through every word of that conversation, in a corridor full of people.
(Safety: gaze engaged, natural blink cadence. He never looks down at his own chest before shot 8.)

— afterwards — she reacts a full beat later, once she has checked the name against herself.
— "…Me?" — asked of her friends, quietly, and genuinely a question.

— the walk — she does not hurry and she does not look back, and holding that costs her everything she has.
— the door — the breath is not brave. It is a girl gathering herself in a corridor where everyone can see her doing it.

carries the transition; shots 2 to 6 are the cafeteria inside Chen's head and carry a distinct grade; shot 7 is
reality again and returns to the normal grade. Normal speed throughout — no slow motion. Shot logic: the part
is a closed loop. It opens and closes on the identical portrait of Chen, and inside the loop the memory shot and
the substitution shot share one identical setup so the audience reads the swap without being told.
OPTICS
Shot 1 and shot 7: 29° diagonal field of view, portrait isolation on Chen. Shots 2, 3 and 4: 47° diagonal field of
view, side-on medium at catching distance, matching the framing of the moment from episode 2 — both bodies
from the knee up, faces in near-profile, background compressed into soft depth. Shot 5: 63° diagonal field of
view, medium wide with the cafeteria floor in it. Shot 6: 35° diagonal field of view, on Chen among the tables.
Lens locked inside each shot.
CAMERA
Shot 1 — camera 1.45 m high, 1.1 m from Chen's face on the arched-door side of the coworking hall; the exact
position, height and framing that ended the previous part. Locked off, no push-in. The transition happens in the
image, not in the camera.
Shots 2, 3 and 4 — one single camera position in the cafeteria, unchanged across all three: 1.5 m above the
marble, 2.2 m from the pair, side-on so that Chen's back and shoulders occupy the left half of the frame in
near-profile and the falling figure arcs backwards into the right half in near-profile, faces almost level with each
other at the top of the arc. Slightly below eye height so the two of them rise against the upper-level arcade and
the statues in their niches. Locked off.
Shot 5 — camera 1.2 m high, 3.5 m back on the same side, wide enough to hold the marble floor, the fallen
figure and the nearest tables in one frame.
Shot 6 — camera 1.55 m high, 1.6 m from Chen, standing among the tables with seated students soft behind

Shot 7 — hard return to the exact position, height, distance and framing of shot 1.
ACTION TIMING
0.0–3.0 — the coworking hall. Jenny is still talking off-frame, her voice still distant. Chen is looking at her and
his stare stops moving altogether. Then the transition begins from his face: a radial blur blooms outward from
the centre of his eyes, the edges of the frame pulling into streaks toward the corners while his face stays sharp
in the middle; the hall's ambience and her voice thin away together. At 3.0 the streaked frame gives way.
3.0–4.8 — the cafeteria, held. The exact moment from last week, restaged: Chen in near-profile screen-left, one
arm already behind Enjee's back and one hand at her side, her spine arched back over his forearm, her long
black hair swung out and hanging, her face turned up to his and his turned down to hers, both of them stopped
in the instant after the catch. Behind them the tables, the seated students, the columns and the statues. It
holds long enough to be recognised and no longer.
4.8–9.0 — the same frame, the same place, the same camera — and now it is Jenny standing there. She steps
backwards off balance, her platform sole sliding on the polished marble, her arms coming up, her weight going
past the point of return, her hair swinging out exactly where Enjee's was.
9.0–13.0 — Chen's hands come off his sides and lift toward her, elbows opening, the beginning of the same
catch the audience has just seen him make. At half extension he stops. The hands change job: they rotate, rise
past her and run back through his own hair, pushing the blond under-layer off his face. She drops out of the
frame he was supposed to fill.
13.0–15.5 — wide. She lands on the cafeteria floor on her right hip and both palms, hair swinging forward over
her face, the fluffy bag skidding two metres across the polished marble. Two students at the nearest table turn
their heads.
15.5–18.5 — Chen standing among the tables, hands still in his hair. He lowers them and looks around the
room, unhurried, checking the seated students one by one, and a small smirk arrives late, after the looking is
finished.
18.5–23.0 — a radial smear snaps inward from the frame edges and clears into his face: the coworking hall,
normal grade, full sound back at once, and Chen seated on the third step in exactly the framing that opened
the part. He blinks twice, comes back into the room, shakes his head once at himself, and speaks.
ACTING TASK — CHEN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep it easy — nobody gets to see anybody trying.
MOTIVE (his fuel): last week in that cafeteria his body did something his rules do not allow, and he has come
back to the tape to prove it meant nothing.
GOAL: run the experiment and get the answer he wants — that he would not have caught this one either, so
catching the other one was nothing.
OBSTACLE: the experiment returns the wrong result. He would not have caught Jenny, which means the reach
for Enjee was real, which is the one thing he cannot file.
TACTIC: in the cafeteria he is not watching Jenny fall — he is watching himself decide, and then immediately
checking the room to see how the decision plays to an audience. The smirk is not cruelty; it is him confirming
he got away with it. Back in the hall he keeps checking the same room for the same reassurance and does not
get it.
Moment to moment:
— the first three seconds — his eyes stop moving on Jenny, which is the only cue the audience gets that he is
going in.
— the memory frame — held, and his face in it is doing something his face never does anywhere else in the
episode: it is completely undefended.
— hands lift — this happens before he thinks, which is why he has to stop it.
— hands into the hair — he is selling the reach as something else, to nobody.
— the scan of the cafeteria — checking faces for a verdict, not for damage.
— the blink back into the hall — the question is still sitting there, and now Jenny has stopped talking.
— "…Nevermind." — he closes the file out loud because closing it silently did not work.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy stare; natural blink cadence.)
PERFORMANCE STANDARD
Chen is performed at the level of a trained screen actor across three different registers inside twenty-three
seconds — undefended in the memory, calculating in the fantasy, and covering in the return — and the same
person must be recognisable in all three. The aborted catch is the hardest beat in the episode and must read
as a decision, not as a glitch: the hands accelerate with real intention, decelerate against that intention,
hesitate for a readable fraction of a second, and then are given a new and deliberately casual job. The falling
performance is real physical acting — the loss of balance starts at the ankle and travels up, the arms reach for
something that is not there, and the face registers surprise before it registers impact. Small involuntary
behaviour throughout, never symmetrical. No snapping between poses, no floating limbs, no head turns
without the eyes leading.
PHYSICS
The catch pose in the memory is a supported lift: his forearm takes her weight across her back, her spine is
arched, her knees are bent under her, her hair hangs with gravity and swings slightly, and both of them are
under real load — his stance is wide with the weight on the back foot. Jenny's fall is a real loss of balance: the
platform sole slides on polished marble, the ankle gives, the upper body goes back and the arms fly out for
something that is not there. The landing is on the right hip and both palms, absorbed and grounded, with a flat
body sound on the marble; her hair swings forward and settles a beat later; the bubble hem compresses on
impact and rebounds. The bag leaves her shoulder mid-fall, hits the floor and slides with decreasing speed, the
bunny plush swinging on its clip. Chen's hands have real inertia — they accelerate toward her, decelerate at
half extension, and change direction with a visible cost. His chains swing and settle. Both radial effects are
optical effects on the image only: nobody's body distorts, nobody's position changes, and no geometry moves.
LIGHTING
Coworking hall, opening and closing shots: cool daylight from the landing windows on one side of his face,
warm chandelier top light on the other, broad soft bounce off the marble, clear catchlights. Cafeteria: tall
daylight from the upper level washes down over the arcade and the statues and keys both faces from above
and slightly behind, with soft bounce off the pale marble floor lifting the undersides of their jaws — the same
light the audience saw on this moment in episode 2. The imagined section runs a half-stop brighter overall,
warmer in the highlights, lower in contrast with a softer rolloff, and the background falls away into gentle
defocus. No lens flare, no glow halos, no colour-shifted dream filter — the difference between the real and the
imagined is exposure, contrast and depth of field only.
AUDIO
Shot 1 opens with the hall ambience at normal level and Jenny's voice sitting behind it, distant and
unintelligible in detail, exactly as it ended the previous part; from 1.4 both thin away together under the
blooming blur. The cafeteria section carries its own ambience — trays, cutlery, a big room with hard surfaces,
voices at distance — but thin and slightly over-reverberant, as memory rather than as a room. The trip, the
landing and the sliding bag are the only close sounds; Jenny makes one short involuntary sound on impact and
nothing else. At 18.5 the coworking hall returns at full level all at once, and Jenny's voice is no longer speaking.
One spoken line in the whole prompt, in English.
21.4 — CHEN, quietly, to himself: "…Nevermind."
No music, no subtitles, no narration, no inner voice-over, no other dialogue.
STYLE
Live-action Korean teen-drama realism with editorial fashion styling. Real skin texture, no beauty smoothing.
Painted plaster, gilded capitals, carpet, marble, rattan and real crystal. Fine film grain, gentle contrast, warm
interior light against cool daylight.

flicker. Natural motion cadence: the fall carries brief directional motion blur and resolves into a readable,
grounded landing pose; no duplicated limbs, no frame-skipping stutter. Both radial effects are clean directional

edges.

ACTING TASK — CHEN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep it easy — nobody in this hall gets to see anybody trying.
MOTIVE (his fuel): being wanted is comfortable and being caught wanting is not; the moment he reaches for
someone, he is holdable.
GOAL: get through the greeting without giving her anything she can count on later.
OBSTACLE: something happened last week that he has not explained to himself yet, and she is standing close
enough to raise the question without meaning to.
TACTIC: he manages distance instead of conversation. Staying seated is the first half of the performance — not
a snub he decides on, just a body that never considers standing an option, and the hug is fast because fast
costs less than slow. Then, while she talks, his attention quietly leaves the hall. This is the important part: he
does not glaze over and he does not go blank. His eyes keep moving in small purposeful ways, the way a
person's eyes move when they are reading something that is not in front of them. He is comparing her to
something, and losing.
Moment to moment:
— through the group conversation — minimum output, chin and eyebrows only, letting the others carry it.
— as she arrives — he registers her and does not move; the delay is the message.
— the hug — quick, one-armed, the can never put down, and he is back in position before she is.
— as she starts talking — for two seconds he is genuinely listening.
— then the switch — the listener's responses stop first, before the eyes change; she keeps talking into a face
that has stopped answering.
— the last three and a half seconds — eyes on her, mind elsewhere, and the question forming behind them is
one he will not ask out loud.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy, unfocused stare; the eyes keep making
small live movements and the blink cadence stays natural. He is thinking hard about something else, not
switched off.)
ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep it easy — nobody in this hall gets to see anybody trying.
MOTIVE (her fuel): she has just spent her lunch break threatening somebody to protect this exact thirty
seconds; it has to look effortless.
GOAL: get a real greeting out of him in front of his friends, because the friends are the audience that makes it
true.
OBSTACLE: he gives her the shape of it and not the thing — she has to bend down to a boy who did not get up,
and it is over before she has arrived in it.

natural end of a lap rather than the reason she came. When he stays seated she covers it instantly by starting
to talk, and she keeps talking — the talking is how she avoids letting the silence report on what just happened.
She works harder and harder for a response and gets less and less.
Moment to moment:
— the wave — wide and warm, playing to the group, no contact needed.
— turning to Chen — a half-second where the brightness has to be re-lit.
— the hug — she is still arriving when it ends; her arms have barely closed before his is gone.
— starting to talk — immediately, without a gap, because a gap would be an admission.
— through her own speech — her eyes go between his eyes and his mouth, hunting for the response; she talks
slightly faster to cover its absence, and laughs once at her own line to give the moment somewhere to land.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

bodies start from the hips and the head arrives last, hands find real objects and real resting places, and nobody
holds a pose. Between beats the characters keep living — a weight shift, a breath, a thumb on the rim of a can,

thought: the eyes change first, the mouth second, the body last. The four friends run a genuine parallel
conversation with their own overlaps, laughs and interruptions, and none of them reacts to Jenny's speech or
turns toward camera. No stiff mannequin stances, no puppet-like limb motion, no snapping between poses.

ACTING TASK — ENJEE (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): get through this corridor without becoming an event.
MOTIVE (her fuel): three weeks ago nobody looked at her at all, and some part of her has been quietly waiting for the visibility to turn out to be a mistake somebody would
eventually come and correct.
GOAL: find out what she has done wrong before she has to walk into that room.
OBSTACLE: she cannot think of anything, which is much worse than being able to.
TACTIC: she searches faces. It starts as an ordinary check of her friends — genuinely hunting for one person who knows why, reading each of the three in turn and adjusting as she
gets nothing — and then it becomes a scan of the corridor as she walks, catching the students who turn away a half-second too late. Every face that gives her nothing confirms
something she does not yet have a word for. Her hand on the strap is doing the only thing her hands can do.
Moment to moment:
— in the circle — warm, quick, slightly careful; she checks after her own joke whether it landed, the way she always has.
— the chime — she turns her head toward the speaker like anyone would, unhurried, expecting it to be about somebody else.
— the announcement — she listens to the whole of it properly, with her whole attention, and does not react while it is playing.
— afterwards — she reacts a full beat later, once she has checked the name against herself.
— "…Me?" — asked of her friends, quietly, and genuinely a question.
— reading the three of them — one, two, three, and the third one's fading smile is the one that finishes her.
— the two seconds of thinking — she is running through everything she has done this week and finding nothing. This is real cognitive work and it shows in her eyes, not in her face:
no performed worry, no lip bite, no bracing.
— the walk — she does not hurry and she does not look back, and holding that costs her everything she has.
— the door — the breath is not brave. It is a girl gathering herself in a corridor where everyone can see her doing it.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy stare; natural blink cadence, including through the two seconds of thinking.)

serious about a second before the others do. After she leaves, they look at each other rather than after her.

Real trip mechanics govern the whole passage. The rigid platform sole does not bend, so the blocked left foot is arrested as one solid unit and the arrest is abrupt with no
give. Her heel lifts and the sole pivots and scrapes against the sneaker with a hard rubber-on-rubber scuff. Her hips lag behind her shoulders throughout the rotation. The
failed recovery step lands with a skid, not a stamp, because the marble is polished. The tray, once released, is a separate object with its own weight and spin and travels
forward and down ahead of her: it turns over, the rice breaks apart as a mass rather than as separate grains, the side dishes lift clear of their compartments, the steel
spoon spins away on its own path, and it lands out of frame with a hard flat slap on marble.
Jenny's chair takes her weight as she drives the leg out and the chair legs shift a few millimetres with a short scrape; the braced leg is rigid and does not give when the
sandal hits it.
Chen's catch is heavy: her full falling weight arrives on his right forearm, his stance widens, his front foot slides a few centimetres on the polished floor and his
shoulder drops under the load before he lifts her back. Her long straight hair swings forward across her face on the rotation, then falls back off it when he brings her up,
and settles several beats late. The lace ruffles of the skirt lift and drop late. The red patent jacket creaks and catches the light in hard flat planes, and his chain belt
and necklaces swing out and settle late. Through the slow-motion passage, cloth, hair, rice and the spoon all move with real weight rather than floating, and nothing hangs
in the air longer than its mass allows.

THE COLLISION IS A BLIND CORNER — FOLLOW EXACTLY
IT IS PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE FOR EITHER OF THEM TO SEE THE OTHER BEFORE CONTACT, and that is what makes the accident real. RYAN is inside the dim side stairwell, walking out through
the arched doorway into the corridor. JENNY is walking fast down the corridor close along the left wall and is turning into that same doorway. The solid pier of wall between the
doorway and the corridor stands between them the whole way in: he cannot see down the corridor until he is already past the threshold, and she cannot see into the dark arch until
she is already inside it. Their sightlines open and their bodies meet in the same instant.
Because of that, neither of them slows, sidesteps, brakes or braces at any point, and neither one turns their head toward the other before impact. Jenny's eyes are already aimed
into the doorway she is turning into. Ryan's eyes are on the corridor ahead of him as he comes out. There is no glance, no double-take and no last-second flinch from either of them.
Only the camera, standing out in the colonnade, can see both of them coming.

full of people. While she is clearing it up, another girl walks past behind her and slips her own pearl bracelet into the open side pocket of the white backpack. She walks away
carrying it. One location, eight timed shots, hard cuts on action only. 20 seconds.

THE LOCKER AND THE GIFTS — FOLLOW EXACTLY
THE LOCKER INTERIOR IS PLAIN AND ALMOST BARE. Bare powder-blue painted metal on all sides, one shelf, and on it only: a short stack of ordinary schoolbooks with plain cloth spines,
one plain cream notebook, a small plain pencil case in solid pale grey, and a folded pale cardigan. That is the entire contents besides the gifts. Every surface inside is smooth
painted metal. The inside of the door is bare metal as well.
THE GIFTS ARE ALL PLAIN, HANDMADE-LOOKING AND UNMARKED. Exactly these things and nothing else:
— five or six small boxes in solid pastel colours — dusty pink, cream, pale mint, pale blue — plain matte card, each tied with a single narrow satin ribbon in one plain colour.
— seven or eight folded cards and envelopes in plain cream, white and pale pink paper. Any handwriting on them is small, soft and cursive and stays illegible at every camera
distance; the cards are otherwise blank paper.
— two small handmade fabric charms on short cord loops: one is a knitted heart in dusty pink yarn, the other is a plain cream wool pom-pom. Both are simple abstract shapes.
— one bunch of pale pink and white carnations wrapped in plain brown kraft paper tied with string.
Every one of these is plain solid colour, matte, and completely unmarked: no printed pictures, no faces, no cartoon or animated figures, no animals, no mascots, no dolls or
figurines, no character shapes, no stickers, no decals, no badges, no labels, no brand marks, no logos, no legible words or letters, no numbers, no glitter and no metallic foil.
The same applies to everything visible inside the locker, on the locker door, on the backpack and on the corridor walls.

THE BACKGROUND STUDENTS — FOLLOW EXACTLY
The corridor is alive with its own morning, and none of it is staged around Enjee. The unnamed students are arranged in SMALL SEPARATE CLUSTERS standing and talking to each other,

further down, another PAIR of boys near a column, and two or three individuals simply walking through. Each cluster is turned inward toward its own conversation, not toward camera
and not toward Enjee. They talk, gesture, shift weight and look at each other continuously throughout the sequence.

FORMAT MODE
Controlled multi-shot sequence, 20 seconds, eight timed shots, hard cuts on action only. Real-time pace throughout with no dead air between shots. NORMAL SPEED THROUGHOUT — no slow
motion, no speed ramp and no time effect anywhere, including on the falling gifts and on the drop. The camera stays inside the right-hand colonnade for the whole sequence and never
crosses to the locker side. ENJEE NEVER TURNS FAR ENOUGH TO SEE JENNY.

ACTION TIMING
[0.0–2.6] Shot 1, the wide. ENJEE turns the handle and pulls. The door resists for half a second, packed from inside, and then gives all at once — the pastel boxes, the folded cards
and envelopes, the two fabric charms and the wrapped carnations come out at her. Two boxes glance off her shoulder and forearm, one lid pops and spins flat on the marble, cards fan
out across the floor around her sandals. She flinches back a full step, the textbook still clamped under her arm, her free hand up. Behind her the clusters carry on talking; at the
sound, two heads from two different groups come round over the shoulder for a second and go back to their conversations.
[2.6–5.0] Shot 2, on her face. The flinch drops out of her and she just looks at it. Her eyes travel over the pile — down to the cards fanned across the marble, across to the
flowers, over to the boxes still wedged in the locker, back down again — and something opens up in her face. A small, real, slightly disbelieving sound: "Oooh..." Her eyebrows go up
and the corner of her mouth goes with them. She is pleased and she has not thought about anybody watching yet.
[5.0–8.4] Shot 3. She crouches and gathers a few envelopes off the marble, turning one over to look at the handwriting, then opens the top card just far enough to read the first
line. Her eyebrows lift again. For a good second and a half she is properly, quietly happy and almost smiles at the card itself.
[8.4–10.2] Shot 4. Then she remembers where she is, and she is the one who kills it. Her eyes come up and go left down the corridor, then right — and behind her, out of two
different clusters, three heads are turned her way over the shoulder while their bodies stay in their own circles; one of them says something sideways to the person next to her and
both look back at each other. The warmth goes out of Enjee's face and she folds the card shut flat against her chest.
[10.2–12.7] Shot 5. She stands, sweeps the boxes back into the bottom of the locker with her forearm and slides the loose cards and envelopes in on top of them, keeping two
envelopes in her hand. She pulls three textbooks off the locker shelf and hugs them against her chest with her left arm. The backpack stays on her back and stays closed.
[12.7–15.7] Shot 6, the locked medium. JENNY comes into frame from screen-right at an ordinary walking pace, eyes forward, both hands at her sides, her right hand loosely closed.
As she passes ENJEE she comes level with the side slip pocket on Enjee's right, and for exactly one step her closed right hand opens above it and lets the bracelet slide in. It
drops into the canvas pouch and stays there. She does not slow, does not look down, does not look at Enjee and keeps walking toward screen-left at the same speed. ENJEE, textbooks
in her arm and her back to the corridor, does not react and does not turn. The clusters in the depth stay turned into their own conversations and nobody is looking at either of them
in this shot.
[15.7–17.3] Shot 7, on JENNY in profile, three or four steps further on. One small closed smile arrives and is gone. She turns in at the classroom door deep on screen-left, passing
the pair of boys by the column without acknowledging them.
[17.3–20.0] Shot 8, behind ENJEE at back height. She pushes the locker door shut with her free hand. "Okay..." She turns and walks away down the corridor into the depth of frame,
past the standing clusters, one head turning after her over a shoulder and going back. Slow push-in on the cream canvas of <<<image_4>>>, the fabric shifting and creasing with her stride
— and low on her right side, at the lip of the side slip pocket, one edge of matte cream pearl is just visible, riding along with her. The shot holds and ends.

ACTING TASK — the scene
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): let nothing here look like anything.

ACTING TASK — ENJEE (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever done anything like this for her, and for about four seconds she lets herself have it.
GOAL: find out who did this and what it says — and then get all of it out of sight before anybody makes it a thing.
OBSTACLE: she is standing in a public corridor, and attention has never once been safe for her.
TACTIC: first she reads the gifts, then she reads the room, and the second one wins.
Moment to moment:
— the avalanche: pure reflex, protect the head and the book. No performed scream and no falling over.
— the look: her eyes actually work — they move object to object across the pile, taking inventory, and each one makes it slightly less possible that this is a prank. This is where
the audience falls in love with her.
— "Oooh..." — small, warm, half laughed, entirely to herself. Not a squeal and not for anybody's benefit, but genuinely delighted.
— the card: she wants to know who. Turning the envelope over to look at the handwriting is the most honest thing she does in the scene.
— the check left and right: this is the acting task made visible. The looking IS the doing — her eyes move from one cluster to the next, hunting for a face that is enjoying this.
She finds two or three heads turned her way and that is enough. Nobody actually laughs at her; she talks herself out of it.
— clearing it up: fast, embarrassed, competent. The warmth is gone and she is hiding evidence of it.
— she never touches the backpack and never looks at it. She is busy, not oblivious, and that is why she misses everything.
— "Okay..." — spoken to herself as the locker shuts, the sound of a girl ticking a task off a list.
(Safety: gaze engaged and moving with the task, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): she needs Enjee gone, and just as much she needs to be a person who did not do this.
GOAL: cross this corridor exactly like somebody who is only crossing a corridor.
OBSTACLE: the one second where her hand is doing something her face has to pretend it is not.
TACTIC: she gives her eyes a job that is not Enjee — the classroom door at the far end of the corridor — and holds it, so that nothing in her face is available to read.
Moment to moment:
— the walk in: ordinary, unhurried, already committed. She worked out the mechanics before she got here, which is why her hand needs no aiming.
— passing Enjee: her eyes stay locked forward on the door. The discipline is the performance — no glance down, no glance sideways, no visible held breath.
— the small smile four steps later: the only leak in the whole sequence, and it is for herself, not for anyone watching.
(Safety: gaze engaged on her chosen point ahead, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

PHYSICS
The locker door has real resistance and then gives all at once. The gifts have varied mass: light card boxes tumble and bounce, envelopes plane and slide, the knitted heart and the
pom-pom drop dead with no bounce, the wrapped carnations hit and spread. A lid spins flat on the marble and rattles to a stop. Enjee's flinch is a genuine weight shift onto the back
foot with her platform sandals sliding a centimetre on polished stone. Her crouch loads onto the balls of her feet with one hand out for balance. Skirt ruffles and hair swing a beat
late on the flinch and again on every turn. The loaded canvas backpack rides on her shoulders with real weight, the soft fabric creasing along the seams and the straps pulling as
she moves; it never comes off her back.
The bracelet has real weight: it hangs a moment in Jenny's closed fingers, then drops the short distance into the canvas side pocket and settles low in it with one soft muffled
contact — no bounce, no ring, no rattle, and it does not fall back out. Jenny's stride does not change speed or length at any point and her shoulders stay level through the drop.
The standing clusters carry continuous small human movement — weight shifting from foot to foot, bags on shoulders, hands moving while talking, one person leaning back against a
locker — so nobody in the frame is ever frozen.

LIGHTING
Daylight from the tall arched window at the far end of the corridor rakes in from screen-left as the key; the crystal chandeliers overhead are warm visible practicals; the pale
marble floor bounces a soft fill up into both faces so their eyes stay readable, including in the low crouch shot. Shadow side falls screen-right on both faces. The final backpack
shot is lit by the same flat corridor daylight, even across the cream canvas, with no separate light on the bag, no light change on the pearl in the side pocket and no change of
exposure as the camera pushes in. No flat frontal fill, no studio key.

AUDIO
THE ENTIRE SOUNDTRACK IS LOCATION SOUND ONLY, recorded in the room: the locker latch and hinge, the papery-card clatter of boxes and envelopes hitting marble, a lid spinning to
rest, a card unfolding, marble footsteps, paper and book sounds, canvas and strap movement, the locker door pushed shut, and a continuous natural wash of overlapping corridor
conversation from the standing clusters — words indistinct, with two distant laughs that are clearly not aimed at her. The bracelet's landing is almost silent: one soft muffled
contact and nothing more. Only "Oooh..." and "Okay..." are intelligible speech, both quiet and to herself; lips stay still otherwise, and no background student says anything
intelligible. THERE IS NO MUSIC ANYWHERE IN THE CLIP, at the head, in the middle or at the end — no score, no song, no ambient pad, no tone. No zip sound. No subtitles and no
on-screen text.

STYLE
Modern Korean teen-drama series look. Editorial pastel production design, clean digital cinema, gentle contrast, true skin tones, very fine grain. Art direction is restrained and
grown-up: solid pastel colours, plain paper, plain fabric, no decorated surfaces anywhere. The final push-in on the backpack is composed as a plain observational hold and nothing is
done to dramatise it — the audience carries the suspicion.

QUALITY
Sharp clarity, stable picture, natural colours, readable faces and eyes, controlled highlights. Natural 180-degree shutter cadence at normal speed: brief real motion blur on the
falling gifts and on the walking figures, resolving into sharp readable frames. No slow motion anywhere. No ghosting, no flicker, no duplicated limbs or objects.
