ACTING TASK — the scene
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): let nothing here look like anything.

ACTING TASK — ENJEE (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever done anything like this for her, and for about four seconds she lets herself have it.
GOAL: find out who did this and what it says — and then get all of it out of sight before anybody makes it a thing.
OBSTACLE: she is standing in a public corridor, and attention has never once been safe for her.
TACTIC: first she reads the gifts, then she reads the room, and the second one wins.
Moment to moment:
— the avalanche: pure reflex, protect the head and the book. No performed scream and no falling over.
— the look: her eyes actually work — they move object to object across the pile, taking inventory, and each one makes it slightly less possible that this is a prank. This is where
the audience falls in love with her.
— "Oooh..." — small, warm, half laughed, entirely to herself. Not a squeal and not for anybody's benefit, but genuinely delighted.
— the card: she wants to know who. Turning the envelope over to look at the handwriting is the most honest thing she does in the scene.
— the check left and right: this is the acting task made visible. The looking IS the doing — her eyes move from one cluster to the next, hunting for a face that is enjoying this.
She finds two or three heads turned her way and that is enough. Nobody actually laughs at her; she talks herself out of it.
— clearing it up: fast, embarrassed, competent. The warmth is gone and she is hiding evidence of it.
— she never touches the backpack and never looks at it. She is busy, not oblivious, and that is why she misses everything.
— "Okay..." — spoken to herself as the locker shuts, the sound of a girl ticking a task off a list.
(Safety: gaze engaged and moving with the task, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): she needs Enjee gone, and just as much she needs to be a person who did not do this.
GOAL: cross this corridor exactly like somebody who is only crossing a corridor.
OBSTACLE: the one second where her hand is doing something her face has to pretend it is not.
TACTIC: she gives her eyes a job that is not Enjee — the classroom door at the far end of the corridor — and holds it, so that nothing in her face is available to read.
Moment to moment:
— the walk in: ordinary, unhurried, already committed. She worked out the mechanics before she got here, which is why her hand needs no aiming.
— passing Enjee: her eyes stay locked forward on the door. The discipline is the performance — no glance down, no glance sideways, no visible held breath.
— the small smile four steps later: the only leak in the whole sequence, and it is for herself, not for anyone watching.
(Safety: gaze engaged on her chosen point ahead, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

contact — no bounce, no ring, no rattle, and it does not fall back out. Jenny's stride does not change speed or length at any point and her shoulders stay level through the drop.

SCENE CONTEXT
Night, the bench outside the dormitory. The film opens on a slow push-in onto the two of them, which eases out and settles. Enjee is already working on the graze on Ryan's cheek with a cotton bud, holding his jaw steady with her other hand. He apologises WHILE she works — two short sentences, one straight after the other, for keeping the truth about his family from her — and it costs him: he is ashamed, his head moves in a small slow shake at himself as he says it, and his voice thickens. She does not stop; she keeps treating the wound and keeps glancing up from it to his eyes. She gives the graze one last touch, takes both hands away from his face, looks at him and answers in one flat sentence. He nods. A short beat. Then the corner of her mouth goes and she adds a condition that lets them both out of it — and he raises it, completely straight-faced. Eighteen seconds, one location, eleven timed shots. Voices and sound effects only; no music.

OPENING CAMERA MOVE — A SLOW PUSH-IN, AT A CALM SPEED
The film opens on ONE SMOOTH PUSH-IN LASTING ABOUT ONE AND TWO-TENTHS SECONDS. The camera starts about 3.2 metres from the bench, holding the two of them a little loose in frame with the steps and the hedge around them, and TRAVELS FORWARD IN A STRAIGHT LINE TOWARD THEM until it is about 2 metres out, where the move eases to a stop on the two-shot. The lens does not change — this is a real dolly move forward, not a zoom, so the perspective deepens naturally as it travels.
IT IS A CALM, EVEN, UNHURRIED PUSH at an ordinary cinematic speed — gentle acceleration at the start, a soft ease-out at the end. IT IS NOT A WHIP, NOT A SNAP, NOT A LUNGE AND NOT FAST. THE PICTURE STAYS COMPLETELY SHARP AND READABLE THROUGHOUT — the bench, both faces and her hands at his cheek are clear the whole way in. There is no streaking, no smear and no motion-blur effect.
THIS IS A PICTURE-ONLY MOVE. THE SOUNDTRACK DOES NOT CHANGE FOR IT AT ALL — the ordinary night ambience runs at a constant level from the very first frame, straight through the push and onward. There is no whoosh, no swish, no air movement, no riser, no impact and no transition sound effect of any kind.
FROM 1.2 SECONDS ONWARD THE CAMERA IS COMPLETELY LOCKED OFF. The push exists only at the head of the film and never returns; there is no further camera movement, drift, sway, pan or push anywhere in the rest of the film.

SPEECH RATE — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS FILM
There are only five short lines in eighteen seconds, and each one has been given more time than it needs. EVERY WORD IS FULLY PRONOUNCED AT A CALM, DELIBERATE, CONVERSATIONAL SPEAKING RATE — roughly three to four syllables per second, the pace of someone speaking carefully to one person sitting close to them. Every syllable is audible and every word is clearly articulated.
Approximate length of each line as spoken:
— "I'm sorry I hid the truth about my family." takes ABOUT THREE AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "It was wrong." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
— "Okay. Just don't hide things from me again." takes ABOUT THREE SECONDS.
— "And you're buying me lunch. For a week." takes ABOUT TWO AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "Two weeks." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
NO LINE IS EVER COMPRESSED, SPED UP, CLIPPED OR SQUEEZED TO FIT. If a line needs a moment more, the silence around it gives way — the words never do. Nobody gabbles, nobody rushes, nobody swallows the ends of words.

EMOTION SLOWS HIM DOWN, IT DOES NOT SPEED HIM UP
Ryan is emotional and guilty when he apologises — and guilt makes a person speak MORE SLOWLY, not faster. The feeling weighs his words down. His voice is low and a little thick, the breath is not quite steady, and each word comes out heavier and slower than his normal speech. He is not agitated and he is not in a hurry to get it over with.

HIS HEAD MOVES WHILE HE SPEAKS — GUILT
As he says the apology he gives A SMALL, SLOW SHAKE OF THE HEAD — a few degrees left and right, twice, aimed at himself, the way someone does when they cannot believe what they did. His eyes drop from hers for a moment on the shake and come back up. His jaw is tight, his throat works once before he starts, and his eyebrows pull slightly together in the middle. Because Enjee's hand is under his jaw, HER HAND MOVES WITH HIM and then steadies him again — she adjusts her grip a fraction to keep the bud on the wound. The head movement is small and controlled, never a big theatrical swing.

ENJEE'S SKIN IS PERFECTLY CLEAR
Enjee's complexion is ONE SMOOTH EVEN TONE from hairline to jaw and down the neck — uniform, unbroken, healthy, flawless. Both of her cheeks are exactly the same clean colour as her forehead and her chin: smooth, matte, untouched skin all the way across. Her hands are clean. The ointment, the shine and the injury belong to Ryan's right cheekbone alone and appear nowhere else in the film.

RYAN'S CARDIGAN IS CLEAN
The pale blue ribbed cardigan is ONE EVEN, UNIFORM PALE BLUE across the entire garment — left shoulder, right shoulder, both sleeves, chest and back are all exactly the same fresh clean shade, as if it came straight out of the wardrobe. The white shirt collar and cuffs are crisp white. The wool colour is continuous and consistent everywhere.

RYAN'S TWO SENTENCES RUN STRAIGHT ON
His apology is two sentences said one after the other as a single continuous thought. BETWEEN THEM THERE IS ONLY A BREATH — under half a second. He does not stop, does not search for the words and does not sit thinking between the two lines. He already knows what he is going to say; he says it, and then he stops.

COVERAGE — CLOSE ON BOTH FACES, AND CUT TO HER WHILE HE TALKS
Nine of the eleven shots are TIGHT SINGLES ON ONE FACE; there is one two-shot at the start and one at the end, and nothing else is wider. HER REACTION IS COVERED AS MUCH AS HIS WORDS — the camera cuts to Enjee's face DURING his apology, not only after it. No two adjacent shots are the same size.
